content.text: {"primary_meaning":"Bondage to sin and to an oppressive, godless world-system, from which God delivers his people in an exodus. In common Christian typology, Egypt is the realm of slavery, Pharaoh represents enslaving power, and departure from Egypt prefigures salvation and liberation.","primary_basis":["Exodus 1:8–14; 5:1–23 — Israel is oppressed and enslaved in Egypt.","Exodus 12–14 — God liberates Israel from Egypt through Passover and the crossing of the sea.","Exodus 20:2; Deuteronomy 5:6 — Egypt is explicitly called “the house of slavery.”","Micah 6:4 — deliverance from Egypt is recalled as God’s paradigmatic act of redemption.","1 Corinthians 10:1–6 — Paul treats the exodus events as typological examples for Christians.","Hebrews 11:24–27 — Moses’ rejection of Egypt is associated with choosing God and enduring for the promised reward.","Revelation 11:8 — the hostile city is “spiritually” called Egypt, explicitly using Egypt as a symbol of opposition and oppression."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"A worldly imperial power characterized by idolatry, pride, and hostility toward God and his people.","basis":["Ezekiel 20:7–8 — Egypt is associated with idols.","Ezekiel 29:3–16; 30:1–19 — Egypt and Pharaoh exemplify proud imperial power brought under judgment.","Revelation 11:8 — Egypt functions as a spiritual name for a city hostile to God’s witnesses."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"False security and misplaced reliance on political, military, or human power instead of God.","basis":["Isaiah 30:1–7 — dependence on Egypt is condemned as a useless refuge.","Isaiah 31:1–3 — those who rely on Egypt’s horses and strength rather than the Lord are rebuked.","Jeremiah 42:13–22 — flight to Egypt for safety is portrayed as disobedient and ultimately disastrous."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Exile or alienation outside the promised land, often contrasted with covenant life and inheritance.","basis":["Genesis 15:13–16 — Abraham’s descendants will live as aliens and be oppressed before returning to the land.","Deuteronomy 17:16 — returning to Egypt represents reversal of the exodus.","Hosea 8:13; 9:3 — “return to Egypt” can signify renewed exile and servitude."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A place of refuge, preservation, or providential shelter during danger and famine.","basis":["Genesis 45:5–11; 50:20 — God uses Joseph’s position in Egypt to preserve life.","Matthew 2:13–15 — Egypt shelters Jesus from Herod before the return that fulfills “Out of Egypt I called my son.”"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"A setting of learning, wealth, and cultural power that may be valued yet subordinated to faithfulness to God.","basis":["Acts 7:22 — Moses is educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.","Hebrews 11:26 — the treasures of Egypt are contrasted with the greater value of sharing in the Messiah’s reproach."],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a settled conventional Christian typology in which Egypt signifies slavery to sin or the oppressive world from which God redeems his people. This is not a universal meaning for every biblical occurrence: many passages refer to the historical nation directly, and other contexts portray Egypt as refuge, false security, imperial pride, or exile."}
